questions.q: Which of these is a bug (a programmer error), not an expected failure?
questions.explain: The other three are operational errors: the client did something wrong and deserves a clear 4xx. A TypeError in your own code was never planned: it is a bug, a 500 for the client and full details in your logs.
options: A client asks for task 9, which does not exist
A client sends a title with only 2 characters
Your code reads task.title while task is undefined, and throws a TypeError
A client tries to create a task whose title already exists

questions.q: What should the client get when a bug happens while handling its request?
questions.explain: The client did nothing wrong, and a bug's message often describes your internals. Keep the details for yourself, in the logs, where you can fix it.
options: A 400 with the error message, so it can fix its request
A 500 with a generic message, while the details go to your logs
The stack trace, so the client can report the exact line

questions.q: Framework errors (SchemaError, HttpError, CircularDependencyError) and application errors (NotFoundError, your own classes) all extend BaseError. Why does that help?
questions.explain: An error handler does not need to know every class. It reads the same fields from any BaseError and builds the right response.
options: It makes errors faster to throw
One piece of code can handle them all: every error has the same fields, such as statusCode, code and expose
It stops errors from being caught by mistake
It is required for try/catch to work

questions.q: A client wants to react when a task title is taken. What should it check?
questions.explain: The code is a stable, machine-readable name. Messages are for people and may be reworded at any time; code that checks messages breaks when you do.
options: That code is "ERR_CONFLICT" (or your own stable code)
That the response took longer than usual

questions.q: By default, expose is true for 4xx errors and false for 5xx errors. Why?
questions.explain: "Task 9 not found" is safe to show. "relation tasks does not exist" or a file path tells an attacker how your system is built, so 5xx messages are hidden.
options: A client error's message is meant for the client; a server error's message often describes your internals

questions.q: What does error.isOperational tell you?
questions.explain: Operational errors are part of normal life (a missing task). Non-operational ones are bugs, the kind you want an alert for.
options: Whether the error has been logged
Whether it is an expected failure (true) or a bug (false)
Whether the server is still running
Whether the error has a stack trace

questions.q: Why does an error handler start with normalizeToBaseError(thrown)?
questions.explain: A BaseError passes through unchanged. Anything else (a TypeError, a thrown string) becomes a hidden, non-operational 500 with code ERR_INTERNAL_ERROR: treated as a bug.
options: To make the error message shorter
In JavaScript any value can be thrown, so catch gets unknown; normalizing turns it into a BaseError with the usual fields
To send the error to the client

questions.q: Why does TaskAlreadyDoneError set its code, category and statusCode inside its constructor?
questions.explain: With the options fixed in one place, throw new TaskAlreadyDoneError(3) always means 409 and ERR_TASK_ALREADY_DONE. Nobody can get it half right.
options: Because BaseError cannot be given options any other way
So every place that throws it gets the same code and status; callers only pass the task id
So the error is faster to create
So the status can change on every throw

questions.q: Which is the best code for your own "task already done" error?
questions.explain: Prefix it with ERR_ and keep it stable: clients will write if (body.error.code === "ERR_TASK_ALREADY_DONE"). The status already has its own field.
options: "ERR_TASK_ALREADY_DONE", and keep it the same forever
A new random code in each release

questions.q: What may you put in an error's metadata?
questions.explain: Metadata can end up in responses and logs. Never put a password or a token in it. The serializers redact secret-looking names as a safety net, but do not rely on that.
options: The user's password, so you can debug login problems
The whole request, including the Authorization header
Facts about the failure that a client may see or the log needs, such as { taskId: 3 }
Nothing: metadata is only for framework errors

questions.q: A client tries to complete a task that is already done. Which status fits TaskAlreadyDoneError?
questions.explain: The request itself is well-formed and the task exists, but it clashes with the task's current state. That is a conflict.

questions.q: Where should the rule "a done task cannot be completed again" and its error live?
questions.explain: The service only says "this task is already done". The status travels with the error, and the same service works from a queue worker or a command-line tool, where HTTP means nothing.
options: In the route, which knows the HTTP status
In the service; the error carries its own status, so the service does not need to know about HTTP
In the schema, with a refinement

questions.q: What is the difference between SchemaError and ValidationError?
questions.explain: Both mean bad input and carry status 400. For your own checks, build the issues with helpers such as requiredFieldIssue and invalidFieldIssue.
options: SchemaError is thrown by a schema's parse; ValidationError is for checks you write yourself, with issues you build
They are the same class with two names

questions.q: Which code should throw HttpError (for example badRequest() or a 415)?
questions.explain: Services throw @zudojs/errors classes that describe the problem in your application's terms (NotFoundError). A wrong content type or unreadable JSON only means something in HTTP.
options: The HTTP layer (routes, readJson, middleware), for problems that only exist in HTTP, such as a wrong Content-Type
The container, when a registration is missing

questions.q: Which pairing is right?
questions.explain: The client needs a code and a safe message. Your logs need everything: the stack, the cause, the metadata. toJSON() gives the full picture, so it must never reach a client.

questions.q: A route answers errors with createResponseContext({ status: 500 }).json(error). What is the problem?
questions.explain: A stack trace shows your file layout, libraries and failing lines: a map for an attacker. Build client bodies from serializePublicError or from chosen fields only.
options: Nothing, the error is safe to send
The error is serialized with its toJSON(), which includes the stack trace, the cause chain and the metadata
The client receives an empty body

questions.q: What does ErrorHandler.handlePublic(error, context) do?
questions.explain: It packs the usual steps into one call: normalize, report (to a logger or an error-tracking service), and build a body that is safe for the client.
options: Normalizes what was thrown, reports it to your reporter, and returns the public body
Sends the error to the client over HTTP

questions.q: Why does the Task API's toErrorResponse report only errors that are not operational or have status 500 or more?
questions.explain: Reports are for things you must act on. Bugs and server failures need attention; a client asking for a missing task is normal life.
options: A 404 is not something to fix; logging every one would bury the real problems

questions.q: Why does every error body in the Task API include the requestId?
questions.explain: The client sees only a safe message. The request id connects it to the full details in your logs, without exposing anything.
options: So the client can retry with the same id
A user can send you the id, and you can find the exact log line for that request

questions.q: A handler answers every error with { message: error.message, stack: error.stack } and status 500. Which list of problems is complete?
questions.explain: Use normalizeToBaseError for the status, serializePublicError for the message, and send full details only to the logs. HTTPS protects the connection, not what you choose to send.
options: Only the stack is a problem
The message of a bug can contain SQL or file paths, the stack maps your code, and a client mistake such as a missing task wrongly gets 500
Nothing is wrong if the API uses HTTPS

questions.explain: DomainError is for a broken business rule (422, category business). ValidationError is for bad input (400).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Anything that is not a BaseError is treated as a bug: a hidden (expose: false), non-operational 500 with code ERR_INTERNAL_ERROR.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A BaseError passes through unchanged, so your 404 stays a 404. Only foreign values are turned into a 500.

questions.q: Someone wrote throw "database down". What does this print?
questions.explain: JavaScript lets you throw any value, so catch gets unknown. Normalizing turns even a string into a real error object: an unplanned 500.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The original error is kept in cause. The client never sees it, but your logs can, so you still know what really went wrong.

options:

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Metadata is copied and frozen when the error is created, so changing the original object later, or the metadata itself, cannot rewrite what happened.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A 404 is exposed, so the public copy keeps the real message and the metadata. It never includes a stack trace.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A database error is a 500, so expose is false: the client gets a generic message and no metadata at all. The table name and SQL stay on the server.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The log copy keeps the real message, the SQL and the stack, so you can find the bug. It still replaces the password: keys whose names look secret are redacted.
options:
relation "tasks" does not exist
SELECT 1 [REDACTED] string

An unexpected error occurred.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both serializers redact keys whose names look secret, as a safety net. The real fix is not to put a token in metadata at all.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A ValidationError is a 400 that carries the issues you built. Each issue has a field and a message.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A schema's parse throws a SchemaError, a framework error that extends BaseError with status 400. isBaseError checks that for any value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: handlePublic reports the error and returns a public body with the real message (a 404 is exposed) and the request id you passed in the context.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The plain Error is normalized into a non-operational 500, exactly the kind you want an alert for. The internal address stays out of the client body.
options:
[report] ERR_INTERNAL_ERROR operational=false
500 An unexpected error occurred.

[report] ERR_UNKNOWN operational=true
500 An unexpected error occurred.

questions.q: Write the class TaskAlreadyDoneError: it extends BaseError, takes a taskId: number, and calls super with the message Task 3 is already done (built from the id), code ERR_TASK_ALREADY_DONE, category ErrorCategory.BUSINESS, status 409 and metadata: { taskId }. The program should print 409 ERR_TASK_ALREADY_DONE Task 3 is already done.
questions.explain: Setting everything in the constructor means every throw new TaskAlreadyDoneError(id) gets the same code and status. The caller only passes the id.

questions.q: Finish complete(id): throw a NotFoundError (Task 5 not found) when the task does not exist, a ConflictError (Task 1 is already done) when it is already done, and otherwise mark it done and return it. The program should print 200, 409 ERR_CONFLICT and 404 ERR_RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND.
questions.explain: The service throws errors that describe the problem; the status travels with them. The caller never has to decide which status a missing task deserves.

questions.q: Finish clientBody(thrown): normalize the thrown value, then return only code and message from serializePublicError. The program should print {"code":"ERR_RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND","message":"Task 9 not found"} and {"code":"ERR_INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"An unexpected error occurred."}.
questions.explain: The 404 keeps its real message; the plain Error becomes a hidden 500, so the file path never reaches the client.

questions.q: Finish shouldReport(thrown): normalize it, and return true when the error is not operational or its status is 500 or more. The program should print false false true true.
questions.explain: 404s and 409s are normal life. A bug and a server failure are things to fix, so only those are reported.

questions.q: Finish checkRow for an import file. Collect issues: requiredFieldIssue("title") when row.title is missing, and invalidFieldIssue("priority", "Priority must be low, normal or high") when the priority is not one of those three. If there are issues, throw a ValidationError("The import file has problems", { issues }); otherwise return "ok". The program should print ok and then 400 2 title,priority.
questions.explain: ValidationError is for checks you write yourself. Collect every problem first, then throw once, so the client can fix them all in one go.

questions.q: Finish toErrorBody(thrown, requestId). Return { status, body }: status is the normalized error's statusCode, and body is { error: { code, message, requestId } } with code and message from serializePublicError. The program should print 409 {"error":{"code":"ERR_CONFLICT","message":"Title taken","requestId":"req-7"}} and 500 {"error":{"code":"ERR_INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"An unexpected error occurred.","requestId":"req-8"}}.
questions.explain: This is the heart of the Task API's toErrorResponse: one body shape for every error, the right status, a safe message, and the request id so a user can report it.

questions.q: This handler leaks the stack and the raw message. Rewrite safeHandler so it returns { status, body: { code, message } } using normalizeToBaseError and serializePublicError. The program should print 500 {"code":"ERR_INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"An unexpected error occurred."}.
questions.explain: The client gets only a code and a safe message. The table name and the stack stay on the server, where your logs can use toJSON().

questions.q: Finish statusOf(thrown) so it returns the HTTP status for any thrown value, using normalizeToBaseError. The program should print 404 409 400 500 500.
questions.explain: ZudoJS errors carry their status; anything else, even a thrown string, is treated as a bug and becomes 500.
